prompt: An idealized two-level atom has only a ground state and one excited state. Which transitions are possible in it?

choices.text: Up from the ground state and back down to it
Excitation only; it can never return to the ground state
choices.why: An excited two-level atom can return to the ground state, by spontaneous or stimulated emission. The two possible transitions are excitation and de-excitation.

choices.text: Transitions to a third, metastable level as well
choices.why: A two-level atom has no third level. Adding one gives the three-level system that the section turns to for continuous lasing.

choices.text: Only radiationless decay between the two states
choices.why: The two levels are linked by absorbing and emitting photons; that is how both pumping and lasing would have to work.

explanation: In the idealized two-level atom, the only possible transitions are excitation from the ground state to the excited state and de-excitation from the excited state back to the ground state. Pumping and lasing would both have to use this one transition.

prompt: Of the conditions the section lists for a laser, which does it explicitly call not crucial, though clearly desirable?

choices.text: A collimated, pencil-like beam
Coherent light, with photons in phase
choices.why: Coherence is the first condition, and the section builds its whole argument on it. The one called not crucial is a collimated beam.

choices.text: Monochromatic light, with one frequency
choices.why: Monochromatic light is one of the conditions the laser must meet. The one called not crucial is a collimated, pencil-like beam.

choices.text: Lasing through stimulated emission
choices.why: Stimulated emission is essential: it is the only way to get coherent light. The condition called not crucial is a collimated beam.

explanation: The section requires coherent and monochromatic light. A collimated, sharply defined pencil-like beam is not crucial but clearly desirable, and high efficiency is also desirable.

prompt: The section judges a laser's efficiency by the ratio of output energy to input energy: the higher, the better. If a laser gives out 0.30 J of light for every 12 J of energy put in, what is this ratio? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: Output/input = 0.30 J ÷ 12 J = 0.025, so only 2.5% of the input energy comes out as laser light. The energy units cancel, so the ratio is a pure number.

prompt: Which process must the lasing transition use for the laser's light to be coherent?

choices.text: Stimulated emission
Spontaneous emission
choices.why: Spontaneous photons are emitted independently, not as copies of a passing photon, so they aren't in phase. Only stimulated emission produces identical photons.

choices.text: Absorption
choices.why: Absorption removes photons rather than producing light. Coherent output needs stimulated emission, which copies a passing photon.

choices.text: Radiationless decay
choices.why: Radiationless decay gives off no photon at all. Coherent light comes from stimulated emission.

explanation: Coherence is satisfied only when the lasing transition occurs through stimulated emission, which produces identical photons of equal energy and phase that travel in the same direction.

prompt: What energy must a passer-by photon have to stimulate emission from an excited two-level atom?

choices.text: Exactly the de-excitation energy, E_2 − E_1
At least twice the de-excitation energy
choices.why: A photon of twice the energy doesn't match the transition. Stimulated emission needs a photon whose energy just equals E_2 − E_1.

choices.text: Any energy, as long as it is in the visible
choices.why: Only a photon matching the gap E_2 − E_1 can stimulate the emission; being visible is neither needed nor enough.

choices.text: Less than half the de-excitation energy
choices.why: A photon below the gap doesn't match the transition. The passer-by photon's energy must just equal E_2 − E_1.

explanation: The passer-by photon's energy must just equal the de-excitation energy, E_2 − E_1. The emitted photon then has this same energy, so the two photons are identical.

prompt: For stimulated emission to occur, when must the passer-by photon reach the excited atom?

choices.text: Before the atom de-excites by spontaneous emission
Only after the atom has returned to the ground state
choices.why: A ground-state atom can only absorb the photon. The photon must arrive while the atom is still excited, before it decays on its own.

choices.text: At the same moment that a pump photon arrives
choices.why: No pump photon is needed at that moment. What matters is that the passer-by photon arrives before the excited atom decays on its own.

choices.text: Exactly one lifetime after the atom was excited
choices.why: There is no special delay. The photon must simply arrive before spontaneous emission has emptied the excited state.

explanation: A passer-by photon whose energy equals the de-excitation energy must approach the excited atom before it de-excites via spontaneous emission. That is why the upper lasing state needs a long lifetime.

prompt: What typically supplies the first photon, the seed, that triggers a collection of stimulated emissions?

choices.text: A photon from spontaneous emission
A photon absorbed by a ground-state atom
choices.why: An absorbed photon is gone. The seed is typically a photon given off by spontaneous emission from an excited atom.

choices.text: A pump photon of a different frequency
choices.why: A photon of another frequency can't stimulate the lasing transition. The seed is a spontaneously emitted photon at the lasing frequency.

choices.text: Heat radiated by the walls of the laser
choices.why: The seed has to match the transition's energy. Typically it is a photon from spontaneous emission in the lasing atoms themselves.

explanation: Typically a photon emitted spontaneously serves as the seed. It passes other excited atoms and triggers stimulated emissions, each of which adds an identical photon.

prompt: According to the section, what goes wrong if the excited state of the lasing atoms has too short a lifetime?

choices.text: Too few atoms stay excited for stimulated emission
The emitted photons come out at a higher frequency
choices.why: The photon's frequency is set by the energy gap, not the lifetime. A short lifetime means atoms decay on their own before passer-by photons can stimulate them.

choices.text: The atoms can no longer absorb the pump light
choices.why: Ground-state atoms can still absorb. The trouble is that excited atoms decay on their own too soon, leaving too few for stimulated emission.

choices.text: Stimulated emission becomes faster than absorption
choices.why: That would help lasing, not hurt it. A short lifetime leaves too few excited atoms around for stimulated emission.

explanation: If the excited state's lifetime is too short, the atoms decay spontaneously before passer-by photons arrive, and there will not be enough excited atoms around to undergo stimulated emission. So the upper lasing state must be long-lived.

prompt: What is a metastable state, as the term is used for the upper lasing state?

choices.text: An excited state with a relatively long lifetime
The ground state of the lasing atoms
choices.why: The ground state isn't excited at all. A metastable state is an excited state that lives relatively long.

choices.text: An excited state that decays within femtoseconds
choices.why: That would be a very short-lived state. A metastable state is an excited state with a relatively long lifetime.

choices.text: A state equally populated with the ground state
choices.why: Equal populations describe the limit of strong pumping, not a kind of state. A metastable state is an excited state with a relatively long lifetime.

explanation: A metastable state is an excited state with a relatively long lifetime. Atoms collect in it and stay there long enough to be stimulated to emit.

prompt: In what range are the typical lifetimes of the metastable states used as upper lasing states?

choices.text: Milliseconds
Femtoseconds
choices.why: Femtoseconds are far too short: the atoms would decay before passer-by photons could stimulate them. Metastable states typically live milliseconds.

choices.text: Nanoseconds
choices.why: A nanosecond lifetime is short, not metastable. The section gives typical metastable lifetimes in the milliseconds range.

choices.text: Hours
choices.why: Hours would be far longer than any lasing state lives. The section gives typical metastable lifetimes in the milliseconds range.

explanation: The upper lasing state must be metastable, with typical lifetimes in the milliseconds range: long enough that many atoms are still excited when passer-by photons arrive.

prompt: The chance that a passer-by photon is absorbed depends on the ratio of ground-state atoms to excited-state atoms. As this ratio gets smaller, what is the photon more likely to do?

choices.text: Cause stimulated emission rather than be absorbed
Be absorbed rather than cause stimulated emission
choices.why: That happens when the ratio is large, with most atoms in the ground state. A smaller ratio leaves fewer atoms to absorb, so stimulated emission becomes more likely.

choices.text: Pass through without meeting any atoms
choices.why: The total number of atoms doesn't change, only how they are split between the states. Fewer ground-state atoms make stimulated emission more likely.

choices.text: Be scattered into a new direction
choices.why: Scattering isn't part of this picture. With fewer ground-state atoms, the photon is more likely to cause stimulated emission than to be absorbed.

explanation: The smaller the ratio of ground-state to excited-state atoms, the more likely the passer-by photon is to cause stimulated emission rather than be absorbed. Pushing the ratio below 1 is a population inversion.

prompt: In a two-level system, what is a population inversion?

choices.text: More atoms in the excited state than in the ground state
More atoms in the ground state than in the excited state
choices.why: That is the normal situation at thermal equilibrium. An inversion reverses it: N_2 > N_1.

choices.text: Equal numbers of atoms in the two states
choices.why: Equal populations are the limit that strong pumping approaches in a two-level atom, but an inversion needs N_2 to be larger than N_1.

choices.text: Ground and excited states that have swapped energies
choices.why: The energies of the levels don't change. An inversion is about populations: more atoms in the upper level than in the lower one.

explanation: A population inversion means more atoms in the excited state than in the ground state, N_2 > N_1. This reverses the thermal-equilibrium situation, in which N_1 is far larger.

prompt: The section restates its conditions for lasing as a comparison between the rates of two processes. Which rate must be the larger one?

choices.text: Stimulated emission must outpace absorption
Absorption must outpace stimulated emission
choices.why: That is the normal state of affairs, and it weakens the light. For lasing, B_21 ρ_(ν)(ν_21) N_2 must be larger than B_12 ρ_(ν)(ν_12) N_1.

choices.text: Spontaneous emission must outpace stimulated emission
choices.why: Spontaneous photons aren't copies of a passing photon, so that would spoil coherence. The comparison is between stimulated emission and absorption.

choices.text: Spontaneous emission must outpace absorption
choices.why: Spontaneous emission isn't part of the section's condition. It compares stimulated emission, which adds photons, with absorption, which removes them.

explanation: The rate of stimulated emission, B_21 ρ_(ν)(ν_21) N_2, must be larger than the rate of absorption, B_12 ρ_(ν)(ν_12) N_1. Then passing light gains more photons than it loses.

prompt: For levels of equal degeneracy, the section reduces the lasing condition B_21 ρ_(ν)(ν_21) N_2 > B_12 ρ_(ν)(ν_12) N_1 to just N_2 > N_1. What allows this?

choices.text: B_21 = B_12, and both use the same ρ_(ν)
B_21 is always much larger than B_12 in lasers
choices.why: If B_21 were larger, a smaller N_2 would do. For equal degeneracies B_21 = B_12, and with the same ρ_(ν) only the populations are left.

choices.text: ρ_(ν) is zero for absorption
choices.why: Absorption needs light, so its ρ_(ν) isn't zero; it is the same ρ_(ν) as for stimulated emission, since ν_12 = ν_21.

choices.text: A_21 cancels out of both rates
choices.why: A_21 isn't in either rate; it describes spontaneous emission. The condition reduces because B_21 = B_12 and the ρ_(ν) values are equal.

explanation: Einstein's relation g_1 B_12 = g_2 B_21 gives B_21 = B_12 for equal degeneracies, and ρ_(ν)(ν_12) = ρ_(ν)(ν_21), since it is the same transition. Cancelling these leaves N_2 > N_1, a population inversion.

prompt: In a two-level sample with B_12 = B_21 and the same ρ_(ν) for both processes, there are 4 times as many atoms in the ground state as in the excited state. How many times faster is absorption than stimulated emission?
explanation: The rates are B_12 ρ_(ν) N_1 and B_21 ρ_(ν) N_2, and everything but the populations cancels, so the ratio is N_1/N_2 = 4. Light passing through is absorbed overall.

prompt: Why can't even a very strong pump produce a population inversion in a two-level atom?

choices.text: Absorption and stimulated emission have the same B
The pump light can't be absorbed by ground-state atoms
choices.why: Ground-state atoms do absorb the pump light; that is how the pump works. But the same light stimulates excited atoms to emit just as readily.

choices.text: Spontaneous emission stops once the pump is switched on
choices.why: Spontaneous emission continues, and it only empties the upper level further. The real obstacle is that absorption and stimulated emission have the same B.

choices.text: Excited atoms are destroyed by absorbing a second photon
choices.why: A two-level atom has no higher level, so an excited atom can't absorb. The pump light instead stimulates it to emit, at the same rate per atom as absorption.

explanation: The pump drives absorption, but the same light drives stimulated emission with the same B coefficient. As N_2 approaches N_1, upward and downward transitions balance, so even an arbitrarily strong pump only brings the populations toward equality.

prompt: Even an arbitrarily strong pump only brings the two populations of a two-level atom toward equality. In that limit, what fraction of all the atoms is in the excited state? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: Equal populations mean N_2 = N_1, so the excited state holds N_2/(N_1 + N_2) = 1/2 = 0.5 of the atoms. Getting more than half, a population inversion, is out of reach.

prompt: For a steadily pumped two-level atom with equal degeneracies, N_2/N_1 = (Bρ)/(Bρ + A_21), where Bρ is the absorption rate per ground-state atom and A_21 > 0. Why is this ratio always less than 1?

choices.text: Bρ + A_21 is always larger than Bρ
Bρ is always smaller than A_21
choices.why: Bρ can be made as large as you like with a strong pump. Even then, the denominator is larger by A_21, so the ratio stays below 1.

choices.text: The pump makes A_21 negative
choices.why: A_21 is a positive probability per unit time and doesn't depend on the pump. Because it is positive, Bρ + A_21 > Bρ.

choices.text: The ratio is set by the Boltzmann factor
choices.why: A pumped sample isn't at thermal equilibrium; this ratio comes from balancing the rates. It stays below 1 because Bρ + A_21 > Bρ.

explanation: Because A_21 > 0, the denominator Bρ + A_21 is always bigger than the numerator Bρ, so N_2/N_1 < 1 for any pump strength. As Bρ grows, the ratio only creeps toward 1.

prompt: For a steadily pumped two-level atom, N_2/N_1 = (Bρ)/(Bρ + A_21). If the pump makes Bρ three times as large as A_21, what is N_2/N_1? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: With Bρ = 3A_21, N_2/N_1 = 3A_21/(3A_21 + A_21) = 3/4 = 0.75. Even this strong pump leaves fewer atoms in the upper level than in the lower one.

prompt: To invert a two-level atom by pumping, what would the pumping transition have to do?

choices.text: Send every decaying atom straight back up
Remove atoms from the excited state
choices.why: That would lower N_2, the opposite of an inversion. The pump would have to send every decaying atom back into its excited state.

choices.text: Excite atoms to a third, higher level
choices.why: A two-level atom has no third level; adding one is the three-level solution. In two levels, the pump would have to return every decaying atom to the excited state.

choices.text: Lower the energy of the excited state itself
choices.why: Pumping doesn't move the levels. It would have to send each decaying atom back to the excited state, which the section likens to reversing a waterfall.

explanation: Inverting a two-level atom would need a pumping transition so strong that it sends any decaying atom back into its excited state, which the section likens to reversing the flow of water in a waterfall. The pump would be working against the lasing transition.

prompt: Why does the section say that, in a two-level atom, the pump is in a way the laser itself?

choices.text: Pumping and lasing use the same transition
The pump light leaves the laser as its output beam
choices.why: The output comes from stimulated emission in the atoms. The point is that pumping and lasing both use the one transition between the two levels.

choices.text: The pump is built from the same material as the atoms
choices.why: The section's point isn't about materials. With only two levels, the pumping transition and the lasing transition are the same one.

choices.text: The pump only works while the laser is switched off
choices.why: Pumping and lasing happen in the same atoms at once. Because they share one transition, the pump works against the lasing.

explanation: With only two levels, the pumping transition and the lasing transition are the same transition. The pump light therefore also stimulates emission, and the pump works against the lasing.

prompt: For continuous lasing action, what does the section say must be considered instead of a two-level atom?

choices.text: A three-level atom
A one-level atom
choices.why: One level allows no transitions at all, so there is nothing to lase. The section turns to a three-level atom.

choices.text: A two-level atom with a stronger pump
choices.why: No pump strength inverts a two-level atom; it only brings the populations toward equality. Continuous lasing needs a three-level atom.

choices.text: A two-level atom kept at a higher temperature
choices.why: At thermal equilibrium N_2 stays below N_1 at any temperature. The section turns to a three-level atom.

explanation: A two-level atom can't be pumped into a lasting population inversion. For continuous lasing, the section turns to other possibilities, such as a three-level atom.
